authentication: none; optional free API key for a higher daily quota
cost_notes: free; no SLA and no commercial support; FDA may throttle or restrict access per its terms
entity_identifiers: UNKNOWN - no GMDN or IMDRF code is carried; the text names are FDA prose
free_tier: free; the whole dictionary is ~7,097 rows, i.e. <=8 pages at limit=1000
historical_coverage: current snapshot only - FDA publishes no effective-dated history of product codes
known_limitations: it is a snapshot without effective dates, so a product code cannot be placed in time - using today's classification for a 2015 clearance silently applies later regulation
product codes are occasionally retired or merged without a redirect field
device_name/definition are FDA prose, not GMDN or IMDRF terms, so cross-market device-family comparison needs separate mapping
a code says nothing about which company owns a clearance; it is a join key, not a company signal
licence: public domain: FDA dedicates openFDA content/data to the public domain under a Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal dedication (open.fda.gov/license/, verified)
rate_limits: documented: 240 requests/min and 1,000 requests/day per IP without a key; 240/min and 120,000/day with a free key (open.fda.gov/apis/authentication/, verified). `skip` is capped at 25,000, so full history requires splitting by decision_date windows
research_value: The dictionary that turns a 510(k)/PMA product_code into a device family with a risk class and a 21 CFR regulation. It is what makes submission-level records analysable per track, and it is cheap enough (one small pull) to mirror in full so no downstream join depends on a second network call.
timestamp_fields: meta.last_updated (endpoint-level only; there is no per-code effective date)
